title: You Press the Button: Eastman and Kodak
summary: A young bank clerk named George Eastman mixed photo chemicals in his mom's kitchen at night. He went on to invent a little box camera called the Kodak that anyone could use: you just pressed a button and mailed it back. Soon even kids had one-dollar Brownie cameras and families everywhere were filling photo albums.

sections.heading: A Bank Clerk with a Kitchen Laboratory
paragraphs: Picture a tall, serious young man walking home through the streets of Rochester, New York, in the late 1870s. By day he sits at a desk in a savings bank, adding columns of numbers in neat handwriting. By night he does something much stranger. He shuts himself in his mother's kitchen, mixes warm gelatin with silver salts, pours the gooey mixture over squares of glass and sets them to dry in the dark. Sometimes he works so late that he falls asleep beside the kitchen stove, still in his clothes. His name is George Eastman, and he is about to change who gets to take photographs.

Eastman was born on 12 July 1854 in the small village of Waterville, New York. When he was about six, his family moved to the growing city of Rochester, where his father had started a business school. Then disaster struck: his father died in 1862, leaving his mother, Maria, to raise George and his two older sisters with very little money. One of his sisters, Katie, died when George was fifteen. To help pay the bills, George left school in his early teens and went to work, first as an office boy and then as a junior clerk at an insurance firm and later at the Rochester Savings Bank. He never went to college. Almost everything he knew about chemistry and machines he taught himself.

Photography came into his life almost by accident. In 1877, when he was 23, Eastman planned a holiday to the island of Santo Domingo in the Caribbean, and someone suggested he bring back pictures. He bought a full outfit of photographic gear and paid about five dollars for lessons in how to use it. In the end he never made the trip, but he had caught the photography bug.

What shocked him was how much equipment one picture needed. This was the age of the wet collodion process that you met in Part 7. A photographer heading outdoors had to haul a big wooden camera, a heavy tripod, a stack of glass plates, bottles of chemicals, a water jug and a tent to use as a darkroom, because each plate had to be coated, exposed and developed while it was still wet. Eastman later joked that the whole kit was a load for a pack horse. He began to wonder whether all of this could be made simpler.

The answer was arriving from England. As you saw in Part 8, Richard Leach Maddox had suggested in 1871 that photographers coat glass with gelatin containing silver bromide instead of wet collodion. Once dry, these gelatin dry plates kept their sensitivity for weeks or months. Eastman read about them in British photography magazines, copied the recipes, and started experimenting in that kitchen. If plates could be made ahead of time, he realized, then someone could make them in a factory, by the thousands, and sell them to photographers. That someone might as well be him.

sections.heading: Dry Plates, a Buggy-Whip Partner and a Hard Lesson
paragraphs: Coating glass by hand is slow and messy. Pour too much emulsion and it runs thick at one edge; pour too little and bare patches appear. In 1879 Eastman designed a machine that spread an even coat of emulsion across glass plates, and he travelled to London, then the centre of the photographic business, to patent it. He patented it in the United States as well. He was still working at the bank, using his savings to rent space and buy chemicals.

In April 1880 he began making dry plates to sell. Business was good enough that he needed a partner with money. He found one in Henry A. Strong, a Rochester businessman whose family made buggy whips and who had lodged in the Eastman family home. On 1 January 1881 the two men formed the Eastman Dry Plate Company, with Strong as president and Eastman as treasurer, though Eastman was the one who really ran things. Later that year he finally quit the bank to work on photography full time.

Then came the lesson that shaped his whole career. Not long after the company got going, photographers began complaining that Eastman plates were coming out fogged and weak. Some of the gelatin he had bought had a problem that ruined the emulsion, and plates sitting on dealers' shelves had lost their sensitivity. Eastman could have blamed the customers. Instead he recalled the faulty plates and replaced them, even though it nearly wiped out his young company. He then spent weeks running test after test until he could make good plates again. Afterward he said that the firm's reputation mattered more than any single sale.

This experience taught Eastman two things he never forgot. First, a factory product had to be reliable every single time, so he became fussy about testing and quality control. Second, he did not want to depend only on selling one fragile, heavy product to professional photographers. He started to dream of something lighter than glass, something that could be rolled up.

sections.heading: Goodbye, Glass: The First Roll Film
paragraphs: Glass has real problems as a home for photographs. It is heavy; a box of plates for a day's shooting could weigh several kilograms. It breaks. And each plate holds only one picture, so you must swap plates in the dark or carry a separate holder for every shot. A flexible material that could be wound on a spool, like thread on a reel, would let a photographer carry dozens of pictures in a pocket-sized roll.

Eastman's first try used paper. In 1884 and 1885 he and a camera maker named William H. Walker designed a roll holder, a small box with two spools that could be fitted to the back of an ordinary plate camera. The patent for this Roll Holder for Photographic Films was issued in May 1885. Inside it was a long ribbon of paper coated with light-sensitive emulsion. After each picture, you turned a key to wind fresh film into place. The company called its paper film American Film.

Paper, though, has fibres and grain. When light shone through a paper negative to make a print, the texture of the paper showed up as a blotchy pattern, just as with Talbot's calotypes in Part 5. Eastman's clever fix was stripping film: the emulsion was coated on paper with a soluble layer in between, and after developing, the emulsion was peeled off the paper and transferred onto a clear sheet of gelatin. It worked, but it was fiddly enough that skilled darkroom workers struggled with it.

Professional photographers mostly shrugged. They were used to plates and saw little reason to change. That disappointment pushed Eastman toward a bold idea. Perhaps the real market was not the few thousand professionals at all, but millions of ordinary people who had never taken a picture in their lives because it seemed too hard. To reach them, he would have to sell not just film but a whole system: a camera so simple that anyone could use it, and a service that would do all the hard chemistry for them.

sections.heading: The Kodak: You Press the Button, We Do the Rest
paragraphs: In 1888 Eastman launched the result, a small wooden box covered in black leather, about 17 centimetres long, 10 centimetres tall and 8.5 centimetres wide. It was called simply the Kodak. There were no knobs for focus and no settings to puzzle over. The lens, with a focal length of about 57 millimetres, was fixed in place so that everything from a few feet away to the far distance looked reasonably sharp. It did not even have a proper viewfinder; you aimed it using lines marked on the top of the box.

Taking a picture was a three-step dance. You pulled a string on top to set the shutter, a rotating cylinder inside the box. You pressed a button to take the picture. Then you turned a key to wind the film forward for the next one. The camera came already loaded with a roll long enough for 100 exposures, and each picture came out round, about 2.5 inches (roughly 6.5 centimetres) across. The round shape matched the circle of sharp light the simple lens could produce, so nothing in the corners would look blurry.

The truly new part came after the last picture. Instead of opening the camera in a darkroom, the owner mailed the whole camera back to the Eastman factory in Rochester with $10. Workers there removed the film, developed it, printed the pictures, loaded a fresh 100-exposure roll and sent everything back: camera, prints and negatives. The camera itself cost $25. That was a lot of money in 1888, about two weeks or more of wages for many workers, so the first Kodak owners tended to be fairly well-off. But for the first time, you did not need any chemistry knowledge at all.

Eastman summed it up in one of the most famous advertising slogans ever written: “You press the button, we do the rest.” He was a brilliant marketer. His advertisements appeared in popular magazines, not just photography journals, and they showed ordinary people, especially young women, happily snapping pictures. Later, a long-running character called the Kodak Girl, a fashionable young woman with a camera, appeared in Kodak advertisements and posters, sending the message that photography was easy, modern and fun rather than a messy job for men in stained aprons.

And then there was the name. Eastman invented the word Kodak himself, and it was trademarked in 1888. It does not come from any language or have a hidden meaning. Working with his mother, he played with letter tiles, hunting for a word that was short, easy to say in any language and unlike any other name. He was especially fond of the letter K, which he called a “strong, incisive sort of letter,” and he liked that his new word both started and ended with one. Other companies made cameras that used roll film, but few had a name that was so easy to remember. In everyday speech, people soon called almost any small camera a kodak.

Success came quickly. In 1889 the company offered a bigger Kodak No. 2 that took larger round pictures, and a whole family of Kodak models followed in the 1890s, including folding cameras that tucked into a coat pocket. Eastman reorganized his business as the Eastman Company in 1889, and in 1892 it became the Eastman Kodak Company. In 1890 work began on a huge new factory site outside Rochester that would become Kodak Park, eventually one of the largest industrial sites in the United States.

sections.heading: Clear Film and a Clergyman's Patent
paragraphs: Paper-backed film had always been a stopgap. What Eastman really wanted was a film base that was thin, tough, flexible and as clear as glass, so that light could shine straight through the negative with no paper texture in the way. The material he needed was a kind of early plastic called celluloid, made from nitrocellulose (cotton or wood fibres treated with nitric acid) softened with camphor. Celluloid was already being used to make combs, collars and imitation ivory billiard balls. Could it be poured into sheets thin enough for film?

In 1886 Eastman hired a young chemist named Henry Reichenbach to find out. Reichenbach experimented with dissolving nitrocellulose in different solvents, spreading the syrupy liquid in a thin layer, letting it dry and then coating it with emulsion. In 1889 the company patented its transparent nitrocellulose roll film and began selling it. Soon all Kodak cameras used the new film, and photographers no longer had to peel emulsion off paper. A few years later, in the early 1890s, Kodak added film rolls with a light-proof paper backing that could be loaded into a camera in daylight, so owners could change film themselves instead of mailing the whole camera to Rochester.

There was a twist. Across the state line in Newark, New Jersey, lived a clergyman named Hannibal Goodwin, the rector of the House of Prayer Church from 1867. Goodwin wanted better pictures to project for Bible lessons and Sunday school talks, because glass lantern slides were heavy and breakable. Working in his attic, he developed his own way of making a clear, flexible film from nitrocellulose, and on 2 May 1887 he filed a patent application for it, about two years before Eastman's company filed for its own.

Goodwin's application crawled through the patent office for more than eleven years, partly because examiners found his descriptions confusing and sent it back again and again. It was finally granted on 13 September 1898 as US patent 610,861. Goodwin hoped to manufacture film himself, but he died in 1900 before he could. The patent passed to new owners and ended up in the hands of the camera and film maker Ansco, a Kodak rival, which sued Eastman Kodak for using Goodwin's invention without permission.

The court battle dragged on for years. In 1913 a federal court ruled that Kodak had infringed Goodwin's patent, and after appeals, in March 1914, Kodak agreed to pay about $5 million to settle the case, a gigantic sum at the time. Accounts differ on exactly who received what, but Goodwin's family and the companies that had backed his patent finally shared in the money. Historians still argue about who deserves the most credit for celluloid roll film: Goodwin filed first, but Reichenbach and Eastman turned clear film into a reliable product made by the mile.

Celluloid roll film turned out to be important for a reason nobody had planned. A long, clear, flexible strip could hold not just 100 separate snapshots but thousands of pictures taken one after another, very quickly. Inventors trying to make moving pictures, from Thomas Edison's laboratory in New Jersey to workshops in Europe, would soon be buying Eastman's film by the roll. The same base material, cut into strips and punched with holes, became motion picture film.

sections.heading: The Brownie: A One-Dollar Camera for Kids
paragraphs: By the end of the 1890s, Eastman wanted to reach an even bigger crowd: children. In February 1900 Kodak launched the Brownie, a simple box camera made of cardboard covered in imitation leather, about 13 centimetres long. It was designed by Frank A. Brownell, Kodak's chief camera designer, and it cost just $1. In Britain it sold for five shillings. A roll of film for it was cheap too, and so was developing, which is how Kodak really made its money: sell the camera for very little, then earn profits from the film people bought again and again.

The Brownie took square pictures 2¼ inches (about 5.7 centimetres) on each side, using a new film size called No. 117. You loaded it yourself, pointed it at your subject and worked the shutter. Its name came from the Brownies, mischievous little elf-like characters invented by the Canadian writer and artist Palmer Cox, whose books and cartoons were hugely popular with children. Kodak put the Brownies on boxes and in advertisements, so children would think of the camera as their own.

How could a camera be so cheap? The Brownie stripped photography down to its basics, the same ones you met in Part 6. At the front sat a single simple lens with a fixed focus, so anything more than a few steps away looked sharp enough. Behind it, a spring-loaded shutter flicked open for a small fraction of a second when you worked the shutter release, fast enough to catch a smiling friend in daylight but not fast enough for dim rooms. There was no exposure dial and no focusing ring. The back of the box came off so you could slip in a roll of film, and a winding key on the side moved it forward after each shot, with light-proof paper wound along with the film to keep it safe. The design was so basic that factory workers could assemble Brownies quickly from inexpensive parts, which kept the price at one dollar.

The plan worked brilliantly. Kodak shipped more than 150,000 Brownies in the first year of production. In 1901 came the No. 2 Brownie, which took larger rectangular pictures for $2. Over the decades Kodak sold Brownie cameras in dozens of models, from a special Boy Scout edition in the 1930s to the Brownie Starflash of 1957, Kodak's first camera with a built-in flash. The very last Brownie, a cartridge model made in Brazil, appeared in 1986, more than 85 years after the first.

The Brownie also changed who took pictures. Children who had never been allowed to touch expensive equipment could now photograph their pets, friends and siblings. Many famous photographers later said their first camera was a Brownie. More importantly, millions of ordinary families, not just wealthy ones, could now afford to make their own pictures.

sections.heading: The Snapshot Revolution
paragraphs: The word snapshot is older than the Kodak. In 1860 the astronomer John Herschel, whom you met in Part 5, wrote about the possibility of taking a photograph quickly, as if by a snap-shot, the name hunters used for a quick shot fired without careful aim. With fast dry plates and roll film, that possibility became real. A snapshot came to mean a quick, casual photo taken by an ordinary person, usually with a cheap camera and with no aim except to remember something.

Think about what photographs had been before. Since the 1840s, most people had gone to a photographer's studio, put on their best clothes, and sat stiffly in front of a painted backdrop. A portrait was a special event, maybe once a year or once in a lifetime. With a Kodak or a Brownie, the camera came to you. People photographed picnics, beach trips, snowball fights, new babies, birthday cakes, first cars, family dogs and silly faces. Holidays now came home in envelopes of prints.

These pictures went into a new kind of family treasure: the photo album. Families glued snapshots onto black paper pages, wrote names and dates in white ink underneath, and pulled the albums out whenever relatives visited. For the first time, ordinary people kept their own visual history instead of relying on a professional to decide how they should look. Historians today love these albums, because they show how everyday people really lived, dressed and played, details that rarely appeared in official records or paintings.

Not every photographer cheered. Some professionals and serious amateurs sniffed that snapshooters were careless, wasting film on crooked, blurry pictures of nothing in particular. Others worried that cheap cameras would put studio photographers out of business. In fact, many studios survived for decades by offering things a box camera could not, such as careful lighting, large prints and formal wedding portraits. Meanwhile, photographic clubs and magazines for amateurs multiplied, and some snapshot takers grew into skilled photographers who entered competitions and exhibitions. Photography had split into two worlds that still exist today: the quick, personal snapshot and the carefully planned picture made as art or as a job.

Snapshots also travelled. Families separated by migration could mail pictures across oceans, so grandparents in Europe or Asia could see grandchildren they might never meet. Soldiers carried photos of loved ones in their pockets. And as cameras grew smaller, people began taking them everywhere. Kodak's 1898 Folding Pocket Kodak, with its fold-out bellows, really could fit in a large coat pocket. Much later, advertisers would invent the phrase “a Kodak moment” for a happy event worth photographing, showing how completely Eastman's company had become linked with memories.

sections.heading: The Right to Be Let Alone
paragraphs: Not everyone was delighted. Before small cameras, it was almost impossible to photograph someone without their knowledge: the subject had to sit still in a studio, often paying for the privilege. Now a stranger with a box under their arm could point it at you on a beach, at a funeral or through a window, and you might never know. Newspapers in the 1890s grumbled about camera fiends who snapped people without asking.

At the same time, newspapers were changing. Cheap, mass-circulation papers competed for readers with gossip about wealthy and famous people: their parties, weddings and quarrels. New printing methods were starting to make it possible to print photographs and drawings based on them in large numbers. Put candid cameras and gossip columns together, and private life suddenly felt exposed.

Two young Boston lawyers decided the law needed to catch up. On 15 December 1890, Samuel D. Warren and Louis D. Brandeis published an article called “The Right to Privacy” in the Harvard Law Review. They argued that recent inventions, specifically naming instantaneous photographs, along with the newspaper business, had invaded the sacred privacy of home and family life. They said every person had what an earlier judge had called “the right to be let alone,” and that courts should protect people from having their private lives and images published without consent.

The article is often described as one of the most influential law review articles ever written. Brandeis, who is thought to have written most of it, later became a Justice of the US Supreme Court in 1916 and kept defending privacy for the rest of his career. Laws and court decisions in the United States and elsewhere slowly built a right to privacy, including rules against using someone's picture in an advertisement without permission. The questions Warren and Brandeis raised in 1890 are still with us today, every time someone wonders whether it is okay to post a photo of a friend online.

By 1900 George Eastman had done what he set out to do: he had turned photography from a difficult craft into something anyone could do with the press of a button. Along the way he had given the world a long, clear, flexible strip of celluloid film. Photographers saw it as a better way to carry 100 snapshots. But a handful of inventors on both sides of the Atlantic looked at that same strip and saw something else entirely. It was exactly what they needed to capture not one moment, but thousands of moments in a row, fast enough to bring a whole scene back to life.

deepDive:
Historians often describe Eastman's real invention not as a single gadget but as a business system. Before 1888, photography was a craft: the photographer owned the chemistry, the darkroom and the skill. The Kodak split the job in two. The customer only aimed and pressed; a factory did everything else. This idea, which business writers sometimes call the razor-and-blades model, priced the camera low and earned steady profits from film and processing. The Brownie at $1 pushed it to the limit, and Kodak's enormous film sales paid for research, advertising and factories such as Kodak Park. The approach was so successful that for most of the twentieth century Kodak dominated film sales in the United States, which helps explain why the company later struggled when digital pictures made film unnecessary (see Part 19).

The celluloid film story is a classic patent puzzle. Hannibal Goodwin filed his application on 2 May 1887; Eastman's company, with chemist Henry Reichenbach, filed later but turned transparent nitrocellulose film into a mass-produced product in 1889. Goodwin's patent was not granted until 13 September 1898 because of repeated revisions. Courts eventually sided with the Goodwin patent's owners, and Kodak paid about $5 million in 1914. Sources even disagree about details such as exactly which company was named in the suit, which is a useful reminder that 'firsts' in invention history are often decided by lawyers years later, not by a single moment in a lab.

Nitrocellulose had a dark side. It is chemically related to guncotton, an explosive, and it burns fiercely once lit. Kodak introduced slower-burning cellulose acetate 'safety film' in 1908, but nitrate stayed standard for professional 35mm movie film until 1951, leading to many fires and lost films (see Parts 11, 12 and 17).

Finally, the Kodak changed what photographs were for. Studio portraits had been formal and posed; snapshots were casual, personal and abundant. Cultural historians argue that snapshots shaped how families remembered themselves, often recording happy moments and leaving out hard ones. Warren and Brandeis's 1890 article shows that the privacy worries of the camera age began almost as soon as cameras became small and fast.
funFact: The very first Kodak camera made round pictures, about 2.5 inches across, and each roll held enough film for 100 of them.

check.a: Mailed the whole camera back to the factory, which developed the pictures and reloaded it
